pages.text:
*Ama's Stall Ledger, Night 55. Bowls sold: 21. Words said: 1 (too many).*

The next night, the lane felt longer. Stretched out like a piece of taffy I had pulled too hard. The stalls were set, the lanterns lit, but the air was thin. Quiet. It lacked the usual hum of plastic stools scraping the pavement and the sharp clatter of chopsticks hitting bowls.

I stood on my stool to see over the counter. My knees bent under the weight. Ama was wiping a table. Her movements were slow. Careful. She was not humming.

"Ama," I said, tapping the counter with my pencil. "We need to adapt."

I took the folded paper from my pocket. It was a drawing I had made at school during math class, using the grid lines to make everything look neat. It showed our stall, but different. The tables were square and white, like the ones in the cafeteria. There was a small screen where the cash box used to be, and the bowls were smaller.

"Customers like fast," I said, unfolding the paper on the counter with a sharp snap. "And clean. And modern. We can have a menu board. No one has to ask what is in the soup. They can just look."

Ama stopped wiping. She looked at the paper, then she looked at me. The pot behind her was silent, and the steam had stopped rising.
pages.image: A small girl in a green jacket stands on a stool at a night market stall, holding out a folded paper drawing of a modern setup to her grandmother who stands by a large steaming pot.

pages.text:
Ama picked up the paper and held it with both hands, her rough, dry fingers resting on the white squares I had drawn for the tables. She looked at the little rectangle I had labeled as the screen, then she looked at me. Her voice was very soft. It was not angry, but it was quiet.

"You want it to be like everywhere," she said.

My stomach dropped. I tried to fix it. "I mean, we can keep the soup. Just the... the speed. And the look. It is just efficiency, Ama. It is business."

But the words came out fast and stupid. I felt the heat rising in my face, and I thought of Jun, and the way he had sniffed the air near my desk. I thought of the three times I had scrubbed my hair that week.

I snapped. "I am embarrassed, Ama."

The word hung in the cold air.
pages.image: Ama, with short silver curls and a flowery vest, holds up a piece of paper and looks at Lin, an eleven-year-old girl with a chin-length black bob and straight bangs, in a dark green padded jacket and a red-and-white checked apron, who stands with a flushed face and wide eyes at a night-market stall counter.

pages.text:
The silence that followed was so loud I could hear my own ears popping. It was not the quiet of an empty room, but the thick, heavy pause before a test starts when everyone is too afraid to move.

Across the aisle, Uncle Feng was still cooking. The sizzle of his oyster oil was very loud. *Hiss. Pop. Hiss.* The smell of frying batter drifted over, sweet and hot.

Ama put the ladle down. She did not throw it, and she did not yell. She just placed it on the counter with a heavy *clank* that sounded like a dropped dinner plate.

"I see," she said.

She turned away to face the big, dark pot. I looked at her back. Her shoulders were hunched, and for a second they looked smaller than I have ever seen them, like a pair of small, tired birds trying to hide under a wing that was too big for them.

"I wanted to disappear," I whispered. I did not mean to say it, but the words were already out in the cold air. "I wish, sometimes, we were different."

Ama’s hands, which had been resting on the edge of the pot, stopped moving completely.
pages.image: Ama, in her flowery vest, stands with her back turned facing a big steaming pot at a night-market stall while Lin, an eleven-year-old girl with a chin-length black bob and straight bangs, in a dark green padded jacket and a red-and-white checked apron, looks down at her hands with regret.

pages.text:
My legs moved before my brain caught up. I ran down the empty lane, past the shrimp-fishing pond where the water lay still and black. The balloon-darts booth sat silent, its bright colors looking dusty and tired under the streetlights.

I ran until my lungs burned, then stopped at the red roof at the end of the lane.

The little temple to Mazu was open. The wooden door was worn smooth by years of hands. I pushed it open.

Inside, the air was cool and dark. Red lanterns hung from the beams, and coils of incense smoke drifted up, thick and grey. On the offering table, three oranges sat next to a cup of tea that had gathered a thin layer of dust.

I knelt on the cool stone floor. I did not know how to pray. I just sat there, breathing hard, my chest rising and falling under my green jacket.

"I didn't mean it," I said to the statue. "I did mean it. I don't know."
pages.image: A young girl kneels on a stone floor inside a dim temple, looking up at red lanterns and a statue, with incense smoke swirling in the air.

pages.text:
The silence broke with a *swish*. A broom was sweeping near the door.

The temple keeper stood in the corner, still wearing his straw hat. He stopped and looked down at the stone floor, not at me. Then he picked the broom back up and began to sweep again, sending dust motes dancing in the thin beam of light that cut through the window.

"Every family has a smell," he said, his voice dry as old toast. "Some of us hide it. Some of us hang it on a lantern."

He reached into his pocket and pulled out a small paper tag and a pen, holding them out to me. I took them, my fingers trembling as I held the tag for a long time, looking back and forth between the pen and the blank space. I wrote nothing.

I walked home very slowly through the cold air, stopping at the corner to press my sleeve to my nose. The smell was there: beef, star anise, and ginger. This time, I cried.
pages.image: A young girl stands alone on a dark street corner at night, holding a small paper tag and a pen, looking down with a sad expression.
